title: Cylinder seal (with caps preserved) with animals and divine symbols

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, 1957
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A small dark stone cylinder with metal caps at both ends. Its surface is carved with animals and symbols, including birds and fish.

context: A cylinder seal made in the Neo-Assyrian period, about the 9th–8th century BCE, from black steatite with its copper or bronze end caps preserved. It is carved with animals and divine symbols and is about 3.5 centimeters long.

descriptions.k: This tiny stone roller has metal caps on its ends. Pictures are carved all around it. Look for birds and fish. When it rolls on clay, the pictures print in a line. What would you carve?
descriptions.g12: This is a cylinder seal from Assyria, made about 2,800 years ago. It is black stone with metal caps on both ends. The carver cut animals and special symbols into it, including birds and fish. Rolled on clay, the pictures would print in a strip. Which animal would you look for first?
descriptions.g35: This cylinder seal was made in Assyria, in Mesopotamia, in about the 9th to 8th century BCE. It is carved from black steatite, a soft stone, and still has its copper or bronze caps at the ends. The carver cut animals and divine symbols into the stone, and the museum's record notes birds and fish. When the seal is rolled over clay, the design prints as a band. Why might an owner want symbols of gods on a personal seal?
descriptions.g68: Made in the Neo-Assyrian period, around the 9th to 8th century BCE, this seal is carved from black steatite and fitted with metal caps that survive at both ends. Its design combines animals, including birds and fish, with divine symbols, signs that stand for gods or their powers. Because the carving is cut into the stone, the design reads correctly only in a clay impression. Seals like this marked ownership and approved goods. How might animals and symbols together tell a viewer about their owner, and what would you need to know to be sure?
descriptions.g910: This Neo-Assyrian seal of about the 9th to 8th century BCE joins craft and meaning in a piece only about 3.5 centimeters long. Black steatite is easily carved, and the surviving copper or bronze caps show how the stone was finished and perhaps protected. The imagery combines animals, including birds and fish, with divine symbols, so one small surface references the natural and the sacred. Some of these symbols are understood from texts and other seals, while others remain uncertain. How does compression of a whole visual world into a rolling band shape what viewers see?
descriptions.g1112: Seals like this one were practical tools of administration and also vehicles for personal and religious imagery. Made in the Neo-Assyrian period, this example in steatite retains its metal caps, a rare detail that reminds us of the object as a whole rather than only its impression. Divine symbols may have signaled protection or devotion, and animals such as birds and fish may carry meanings we cannot fully recover. Scholars interpret such combinations cautiously, comparing many seals. How do we balance the evidence of the object with comparative reading, and what do we risk when we assign fixed meanings to symbols?

teacherNote.context: A Neo-Assyrian cylinder seal with its metal caps preserved, rolled on clay to mark ownership. The museum record notes animals and divine symbols; students should note that the exact meaning of the symbols is interpreted by comparison with other objects.
directions: Have students roll a cylinder such as a marker over modeling clay and design a pattern of animals that works when repeated.
Discuss how a symbol can stand for an idea, and ask students to invent symbols for a class value.
Compare this seal with other seals in the archive and discuss similarities in animals and materials.
